Imagine you are the marketing director of a company. You have to create a survey in order to get insight on your new company slogan.

Instructions:

Write a 200 - 220 word survey.
Start by answering the following three questions:

  • What do you want to know?
  • Who are you going to ask?
  • How are you going to conduct the survey?

    • Then, write at least 10 questions. Use a combination of open-ended and closed questions.
    Finally, state how you will analyze and present the results.

    When you have typed in ALL your answers, click the Go to Writing Task button.

    My Professional Survey

Let's review your survey.

Your survey should include:

A clear purpose (what you want to know)
A target audience (who you are going to ask)
A format (how are you going to conduct the survey)
A combination of open-ended and closed questions (what you are going to ask)
An analysis (how you are going to analyze the results)

Proofread your survey for spelling, grammar and punctuation errors.

Click the Submit button to save your survey.

images.text:
Peter: Hello, my name is Peter Smith. This a survey on Holly's. The purpose of the survey is to get insight on brand awareness, the name of the company, and the company's philosophy. Do you have a minute to answer some questions?
Shopper: Alright.
Peter: What are your impressions of Holly's apparel?
Shopper: I'm a great believer in their products.
Peter: How about the company itself?
Shopper: I don't know. Honestly, I never think about companies.

Peter: Have you heard any news about child labor connected with Holly's?
Shopper: To be honest, I don't listen to the news. But I'm sure that if I heard something about child labor I wouldn't buy it. Is there a problem?
Peter: No. There were some concerns but Holly's is acting responsibly about that.
Shopper: Good.
Peter: So, you don't think too much about the company's objectives and priorities?
Shopper: Well, I suppose any company wants to have a good product and make profit. The way I see it, not too many companies approach customers with surveys. So maybe Holly's cares about connecting with consumers.
Peter: Good thoughts. I'm almost done here. We're looking at our company's image and wondering whether it reflects our philosophy to the public. What do you think of the name?

Shopper: Ummm, who's Holly?
Peter: Ha ha!
Shopper: Seriously!
Peter: I, uh, don't know.
Shopper: Well there you have it.
Peter: I guess so. Well, thank you for your time. By the way, don't forget to look up our website next month to learn more about what Holly's will be doing beyond simple product ­for ­profit.
Shopper: Sounds good!

Conversations are far more interesting when people interact during the conversation. It is important to ask for others' opinions on a subject as well as giving your own.
Here are some ways you can give opinions.

• I'm a great believer in ...
  • Honestly, ...
  • To be honest, ...
  • I'm sure that ...
  • I suppose ...
  • The way I see it, ...
The way I see it, not many companies actually ask consumers how they feel about their products.
I'm a great believer in what they do.
Honestly, I never think too much about that.
To be honest, I don't actually follow the news.
A survey allows you to gather information quickly on a topic of your interest. When creating a survey, it is important to ask the right questions so as to gather customer feedback effectively.
When forming questions in English, it is easy to follow the formula called QUASM. That is QU (=QUestion word), A (=Auxiliary verb), S (=Subject) and M (=Main verb).
This formula applies to any question in English.

Get together in a group of four.
Two people will argue that a corporation must be ethically responsible to influence the public.
The other two people will argue that it is the public that must be ethically responsible first and influence corporations.
Each side must develop four or five supporting arguments.
Once the arguments are ready, take turns debating.
When you cannot think of any more arguments, end the debate and decide which team had the most convincing arguments.
